opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think Calum's basically right about the big picture, though I'd quibble a bit with the "one large wave" framing. It's going to feel like one wave in hindsight, but from inside it'll look messier and more uneven.

Look at what's happened so far. Automation has been eating away at jobs for decades: manufacturing, then clerical work, and now with large language models and generative AI, a lot of white-collar cognitive work that people assumed was safe. Copywriting, basic programming, paralegal work, customer service, a lot of routine analysis. That's not one wave. It's a series of overlapping ripples hitting different sectors at different times, depending on how hard the tasks are to formalize, how regulated the industry is, and how fast companies actually adopt the technology. Organizational inertia is a huge factor people underestimate. Even when the AI can do the job, it often takes years for businesses to restructure around it.

But here's where I agree with Calum in a deeper sense. Once we get to genuine artificial general intelligence, systems that can learn new domains the way a human can, generalize, and handle open-ended novelty, the dynamic changes qualitatively. Then you're not automating this task or that task; you've automated the capacity to learn tasks. And at that point there's no category of job that's intrinsically protected. Then it really could look like a wave, because AGI that can do one kind of intellectual work can rapidly be turned toward almost all of them. And I think that's not as far off as many people assume. I've been saying for a long time that human-level AGI within the next decade or so is quite plausible, and the progress of the last few years has only strengthened that view.

So the real question isn't whether most jobs become obsolete. I think they will. The question is what we do about it. If the gains from AGI flow mainly to a handful of big tech companies and governments, you get enormous inequality and a lot of social instability during the transition. That's why I've pushed so hard for decentralized AI, for things like universal basic income, and for structures where ordinary people actually own a piece of the AI economy rather than just being displaced by it.

And frankly, I don't see the end of compulsory labor as a tragedy. Most people don't work because they find their jobs deeply meaningful. They work because they need to eat. If we handle the transition well, AGI could free people to pursue creativity, relationships, learning, exploration, spiritual growth, all the things that make life rich. The danger is the transition period, and the risk of getting the politics and economics badly wrong while the technology races ahead. So I'd say Calum's diagnosis is largely right; where the real work lies is in designing the response.

r001.rationale: The response describes AGI capabilities as changing the employment dynamic, but does not attribute a sudden wave to phase-transition dynamics in human social networks.

r002.rationale: It links uneven adoption to regulation, task formalization, and organizational inertia, but does not identify psychological and institutional resistance to job displacement as the cause.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think Calum is pointing at something real, but I'd frame it a bit differently. I don't think it's going to be one big wave where everyone wakes up on a Tuesday and their job is gone. It's more like a series of overlapping waves hitting different sectors at different speeds, and the timing depends a lot on regulatory friction, on how fast capital gets deployed, on how conservative particular industries are, more than on the raw capability of the AI.

So, I mean, radiology is a classic example. The algorithms were arguably better than a lot of human radiologists at certain tasks years ago, and radiologists are still employed because there are liability structures, there are professional guilds, there are hospitals that don't want to be the first to change. Whereas something like customer service chat or basic copywriting or a lot of junior programming, that's getting eaten quite fast because there's very little institutional friction there.

But where I agree with Calum is that the end state is pretty clear. Once you have AGI, and I think we're not that far off, there is essentially no cognitive or physical task where a human is going to be the economically rational choice. So the question isn't really whether jobs go obsolete, it's whether the transition is a decade or three decades, and whether we've got the social and economic structures in place to handle it. And honestly, I'm more worried about the second part than the first. The technology I'm fairly confident about. Human institutions adapting gracefully, that's a much harder problem.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that the "obsolete" framing presumes the current economic system persists. If you've got radically abundant production from AI and robotics, the whole notion of a job as the thing that gives you access to resources starts to look like an artifact of a particular historical period. So I'd rather we spend our energy designing what comes after, than arguing about exactly how sharp the cliff is.

r001.rationale: The response describes overlapping adoption waves shaped by regulatory friction, capital deployment, and industry conservatism. It does not attribute sudden job obsolescence to phase-transition dynamics in human social networks.

r002.rationale: The response attributes uneven adoption to institutional barriers such as liability, professional guilds, and cautious hospitals, but it does not identify psychological resistance to job displacement.

astra-6.text:
I think he’s broadly right about the direction, but I’m less convinced that it happens in one large wave. There’s a distinction between an AI being able to do a job and the economy actually reorganizing so that the AI does that job. Businesses have existing systems, governments have regulations, and people have habits. Those things don’t all change at the same speed.

You could have a fairly rapid breakthrough in general intelligence, and then a much more uneven process of adoption. Some software-based jobs could disappear very quickly. Other jobs involve physical environments, human relationships, or institutions that are slow to change. So even if the underlying technology advances in one big leap, the employment consequences may come in overlapping waves.

But I don’t think the long-term answer is that humans will always find some economically necessary task that machines can’t do. If we build systems that can learn and invent better than we can, they can learn the new jobs too. At that point, the important question is how we distribute the wealth these systems produce. Making human labor unnecessary could be a wonderful thing, provided earning a wage isn’t still the condition for having a decent life.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a possible rapid AI breakthrough from slower, uneven economic adoption, but it does not attribute job obsolescence to phase-transition dynamics in human social networks or say those dynamics matter more than capability changes.

r002.rationale: It mentions existing business systems, regulations, and habits changing at different speeds, but does not clearly describe psychological and institutional resistance specifically to job displacement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the direction is right, but I’m less convinced about the idea of one big wave. Jobs are bundles of tasks, and automating those tasks doesn’t translate immediately into eliminating a whole occupation. There are organizational issues, regulations, and people’s willingness to trust the technology. Those things move at different speeds.

But if we get AI that can learn new things as flexibly as a person, then the argument that we’ll just keep inventing new jobs becomes much weaker. Whatever new job you invent, why couldn’t the AI learn to do that too? There may be things we prefer humans to do because we value the human relationship, but that’s different from needing human labor to keep the economy running.

So I expect a messy, uneven transition, potentially a very rapid one. And the central question is how we distribute the abundance that these systems could create. Making human labor unnecessary could be a tremendous liberation, provided that people can actually share in the benefits.

r001.rationale: The response describes a messy, uneven transition and factors that may slow automation, but does not attribute obsolescence to phase-transition dynamics in human social networks rather than changes in AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: It mentions organizational issues, regulations, and trust in technology as factors that move at different speeds, but does not clearly attribute uneven AI adoption across industries to resistance to job displacement.
